title: Nothing to hand over: MFA and passkeys

narration: The site asks for a code from your phone.
beats.visual_intent: the exchange that holds for the whole lesson: a laptop on the left, the site as a door on the right, one line between them. The password token travels the line on 'password'; a code token rises from a phone beside the laptop on 'code' and follows it; the door opens

grounding.claim: the everyday sign-in is a generic illustration

narration: That second step stops a lot.
beats.visual_intent: the exchange holds still, door open; the line between laptop and door brightens as the one thing in question, everything else dims

grounding.claim: a second factor stops most account compromise
a second factor does not stop every attack

narration: A password is something you know.
beats.visual_intent: a magnifier on the password token as it sits on the line: only a row of characters, nothing tying it to this laptop; a second, distant laptop fades in at the frame edge on 'any device'

grounding.claim: a password is something you know
anyone who knows the password can use it from any device and the site cannot tell

beats.visual_intent: a copy of the password token peels off and travels from the distant laptop along a second line to the same door; the door opens for the copy exactly as it did for you

grounding.claim: the leak and the replay are an invented example
a stolen password works for whoever types it
bots replaying leaked passwords are the common case Google reports

narration: MFA asks for two different kinds of proof.
something you have, like your phone,
beats.visual_intent: back to the single exchange; three slots stand beside the door and fill on their words, the password token, the phone, a fingerprint; the know and have slots become two locks on the door

grounding.claim: MFA asks for two or more different kinds of proof: know, have, are

narration: The code is on your phone,
beats.visual_intent: the copy travels the second line again and opens the first lock; the second lock waits; the code lights up on your phone beside your laptop, far from the copy; the copy bounces off the door

grounding.claim: with MFA on, a stolen password alone does not get the thief in
the replay is the same invented example

narration: Microsoft researchers found MFA cut the risk
of compromise by a little over 99 percent.
Their own data, not a guarantee.
beats.visual_intent: a meter mounted on the door fills to just over 99 on the spoken number, the study's owner labelled under it in small type; on 'not a guarantee' a thin unfilled sliver at the top stays visible

grounding.claim: a Microsoft study found MFA cut the risk of compromise by a little over 99 percent
it is the vendor's own data and a reduction, not a guarantee

narration: Say a link opens a page
You type your password, then your code.
beats.visual_intent: a second box slides into the line between laptop and door, splicing it in two; it wears the door's face exactly; your password and code tokens leave the laptop and travel toward it

grounding.claim: the look-alike page is an invented example of a common technique
phishing pages copy real login pages and collect the password and code

beats.visual_intent: everything freezes with both tokens poised at the edge of the look-alike box; the frame rests in silence

grounding.claim: the question sets up the relay shown next

recall.prompt: MFA is on. You type your password and your code into a page that only looks real. Does the thief get in?
recall.answer: Yes: the page passes both to the real site while the code is still valid.

beats.misconception: once MFA is on, a phishing page cannot get into my account

narration: The fake page passes each one on,
while the code is still valid.
beats.visual_intent: a magnifier settles on the look-alike box: the password token goes in one side and straight out the other to the real door, then the code does the same; the door opens, and the open line now runs to the look-alike box, not to your laptop

grounding.claim: a phishing page relays the password and code to the real site while the code is valid

beats.misconception: once MFA is on, a phishing page cannot get into my account

narration: The code felt like yours alone.
and what you read, a page can ask for.
beats.visual_intent: the magnifier moves onto the code token: plain characters, the same copyable look the password had in run one, the two set side by side

grounding.claim: a code you read and type can be collected by a fake page

beats.misconception: once MFA is on, a phishing page cannot get into my account

narration: It lives on your phone or a security key,
unlocked by fingerprint, face or PIN.
beats.visual_intent: a cutaway of the phone: inside, a sealed key sits in its own compartment; a fingerprint touches the glass and the compartment lights, the key does not move

grounding.claim: a passkey is kept on a phone, computer or security key and unlocked like the device

narration: The site sends a fresh challenge.
beats.visual_intent: the exchange returns with the cutaway phone in place of the code: a challenge token travels from the door to the phone, the sealed key stamps it, the signed answer travels back; the key itself never leaves its compartment

grounding.claim: the site keeps no shared secret and the device signs a fresh challenge

narration: with the address of the page that asked.
beats.visual_intent: the magnifier settles on the signed answer; an address stamp presses onto it on 'address' and stays, the one saturated thing in frame

grounding.claim: the signed answer includes the address of the page that asked

narration: Your passkey will not answer a look-alike.
beats.visual_intent: the look-alike box splices into the line again and sends its request to the phone; the sealed key stays dark, no answer token forms; the box's line onward to the real door stays empty and the door stays shut

grounding.claim: a passkey made for one site cannot be used by a look-alike site
with a passkey there is nothing a fake page can collect and pass on
the fake page is the same invented example

recall.prompt: Run one: a copied password works from anywhere. Run four: a passkey answer works in one place only.

narration: Against targeted attacks, a texted code blocked 76 percent,
With security keys alone, no one fell.
beats.visual_intent: a ladder of three rungs builds beside the door; the first rung fills to 76 on its word, the second to 90 on its word, the third lights with a counter reading none fallen; the source label sits under the ladder

grounding.claim: a texted code blocked 76 percent of targeted attacks in Google's study
a phone prompt blocked 90 percent of targeted attacks in Google's study
no security-key-only user fell to targeted phishing

narration: Their accounts, so read the direction.
and any second factor beats none.
beats.visual_intent: the whole ladder stays; every rung keeps its fill and the first rung, the texted code, is the one accent on 'any second factor'

grounding.claim: the study rates are Google's accounts and show direction, not a general rate
phishing-resistant is not unbreakable
any MFA is better than none

beats.misconception: texted codes can be phished, so they are not worth turning on

narration: Last, a prompt you did not start.
Say it comes again, and again.
beats.visual_intent: the opening exchange returns with your laptop closed; the phone lights with an approve prompt, then a second, then a third, stacking

grounding.claim: repeated prompts are sent by attackers who already have the password
a prompt you did not start can mean someone else is signing in
the moment is invented

beats.misconception: an unexpected sign-in prompt is a glitch, and tapping Accept makes it go away

narration: asking you to finish their sign-in.
beats.visual_intent: the stacked prompts resolve into one refusal; behind the phone the look-alike box from run three fades in briefly at the end of the line and the door stays shut

grounding.claim: the safe move is to refuse an unrequested prompt
accepting a pushed prompt grants the attacker access

recall.prompt: A prompt you did not start is the relay from run three, asking you to finish it.

beats.misconception: an unexpected sign-in prompt is a glitch, and tapping Accept makes it go away

narration: The passkey answer fits one site.
beats.visual_intent: the opening exchange from b01, now readable: each token gets its label on its word, the password, the code, and the stamped passkey answer that replaces them

grounding.claim: a password can be copied
a code can be relayed
a passkey only works for its site

narration: Refuse what you did not start.
on_screen: refuse what you did not start
beats.visual_intent: three short lines set one by one on their words beside the held exchange; each line lands on the token it changes

grounding.claim: turn on any second factor, it beats none
a passkey is phishing-resistant
refuse prompts you did not start

narration: there is nothing to hand over.
beats.visual_intent: the exchange rests with the sealed key inside the phone and the door shut to everything but it

grounding.claim: with a passkey there is nothing to type or pass on
